old/information-kalman-filter.html.title: Information Kalman Filter
old/information-kalman-filter.html.description:
Based on Gaussian Information Aggregation, assume that we have two sources of information. Process/prediction Equation Sensor/observation Equation We desire to obtain an estimation of , , based on the information provided by the estimate of and estimate of measurements , inputs at two consecutive time steps , and of the modelling errors and . We asume that the knowledge that we have about these variables is statistical even if the underlying physical variable is deterministic ( perspective that we adopt): Noise is Gaussian white, and different noise sources are independent:
We cast these equations so they resemble the form used in Old/Gaussian Information Aggregation Lemma: So, for the process equation:Note that the measurement is obtained through the filter itself, and therefore it is the estimation of the Kalman filter at , : That is, a stochastic variable. Analogously, is the measurement of the input, so it is in general stochastic. Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the prediction equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.The sensor equation is reordered as: so,Therefore: From which:Notice that is the information coming from the use of the observation equation; this is addressed making to make explicit the origin of the information.Finally, the estimate is: In summary: from which If ( has maximum row rank), then:Notice that this is the estimation of the projection of the state onto the row space of (see figure):
The figure depicts the projection of the state () onto the hyperplane (greenish) expanded by the row space of (). In this way, the estimator can be said to be: "The FIM weighted average of the estimations of the prediction and observation estimations." We can retrieve this interpretation when by splitting the set of observation equations into subsets:where have each one maximum row rank. Now we have several sources of information to aggregate: For each of them Therefore from which Note also that even if , we can write: This equation is a very convenient form to look at the sensor fusion, as it allows to integrate sensors separating them into groups. This can be of interest when having different frequencies for different measurements or predictions of states, or when a sensor or prediction equation may fail. It also makes easy the parallel computation or distribution of the measurements and predictions on different nodes. This robustifies the setup because it easily allows removing different sources of information if they are not available.

information-kalman-filter.html.title: Information Kalman Filter
information-kalman-filter.html.description:
Based on Gaussian Information Aggregation Lemma, assume that we have two sources of information. Process/prediction Equation Sensor/observation Equation We desire to obtain the estimation based on the information provided by the estimations of , , and . We explicitly define the statistical properties of our state, observations, and physical modeling errors as Gaussian random variables:(Note regarding notation: While we rigorously track the estimated mean of the state as $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\mathbf{x}} and inputs directly—without a hat—in place of their formal mean estimators. Because these are direct observations, their estimated means are coincident with the measurements themselves)._We assume strictly that noise is Gaussian white, and all different noise sources and estimators are mutually independent:

notation-guide-for-information-kalman-fi.title: Notation Guide for Information Kalman Filter Framework
notation-guide-for-information-kalman-fi.description:
This document defines the strict notational conventions used across the Gaussian Information Aggregation framework. The notation is deliberately designed to adhere to an Epistemic View, where the equations track our evolving state of knowledge (belief) rather than just physical mechanics, adhering strictly to a Maximum Likelihood (ML) perspective.In this framework, the primary variables (, , and ) are always treated as random variables, regardless of the origin of their randomness. Their probability density functions (pdfs) and variances represent our degree of knowledge or epistemic uncertainty about the specific physical realization we are observing.
Standard math font (): Denotes the epistemic random variable itself. The "Hat" (): Strictly denotes the estimated mean of a knowledge state. Because it is derived from noisy data and uncertain models, any variable with a hat is rigorously treated as a random variable. (Note regarding notational license: While we rigorously track the estimated mean of the state as $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\mathbf{x}} and inputs directly in the equations. Because these are direct observations, their estimated means are coincident with the measurements themselves)._The framework linearizes nonlinear systems into matrices (Jacobians). In the epistemic view, the noises ( and ) do not represent raw hardware noise (which is handled by the variance of the sensors themselves), but rather our uncertainty regarding the mathematical models.To unify the treatment of predictions and observations, any equation that provides mathematical insight into the state is generalized as an "Information Source" ().We make a strict distinction between the abstract random variable (which retains model noise to facilitate variance/correlation expansion) and its evaluated estimator (which drops the zero-mean noise for numerical computation).Example Definitions (Prediction):
The Source: The Estimator: The framework uses standard covariance definitions alongside Fisher Information operators. The subscript of a covariance matrix dictates the random variables being evaluated.When information sources are correlated (), they cannot be directly added. The framework uses the Schur complement to orthogonalize one source with respect to the other prior to additive fusion. The "Tilde" ( ) denotes these decorrelated, orthogonalized quantities.

epistemic-interpretation-of-the-kalman-f.title: Epistemic Interpretation of the Kalman Filter Process Equation
epistemic-interpretation-of-the-kalman-f.description:
1. The Ensemble View of the Process EquationIn this classical ontological view, the equation governs the statistical ensemble of all possible realizations of a physical experiment. The variables , , and are treated as random variables representing actual physical variations.Here, a single, particular realization of this equation represents the physical reality. In that specific run, and assume concrete, deterministic physical values. However, across different realizations (if the experiment were to be repeated under identical macroscopic conditions), they will take on different values. Consequently, has different "random" values across the ensemble. This randomness is driven entirely by true, physical variations across repetitions.The Problem of InferenceThe problem of how to perform inference with this formula begins as soon as we concede:
"We don't know the exact initial realization of " "We don't know the exact physical realization of or in our specific experiment" The only things we know are their statistical properties across the physical ensemble, encoded as probability density functions (pdf). For instance:From here, we can begin to make statistical inferences. By expanding the process equation step-by-step, we obtain a precise statistical description of . In the ontological view, this description is firmly anchored in physical reality, because the distributions and variances () represent the actual frequency and magnitude of physical fluctuations across real repeated experiments.2. The Epistemic Shift (Knowledge View)While the ensemble view provides a physical basis for the distributions, we frequently face scenarios where a physical variable is strictly deterministic (a constant) in reality, but its value is unknown to us.Instead of inventing separate notations for "true reality" vs. "our knowledge", we undergo an epistemic shift in interpretation while keeping the exact same mathematical variables. The probability distributions no longer strictly need to represent the frequency of outcomes across physical experiments. Instead, the random variables represent our degree of knowledge about the specific physical realization we are currently observing.If the underlying state is a deterministic constant, its physical variance is zero. However, because we do not know its value, we assign it a pdf (e.g., ). This pdf lives within our algorithm; and are parameters of our belief.This epistemic paradigm seamlessly adopts the math of the ensemble view. If our assigned statistics perfectly match physical frequencies, the filter tracks the true physical ensemble. If they represent pure belief bounds, the computed distributions seamlessly track the evolution of our knowledge.3. Showing the Paradox with Deterministic InputsAssume that ambient temperature enters the system as the input . In our specific realization, temperature is a deterministic physical constant. However, we only know the temperature through a noisy sensor.If we strictly maintain the ontological view, the input has no physical variance. But to perform mathematical inference about the future state, we must extend our interpretation of the process equation to be strictly epistemic. We must treat the input within the equation itself as a random variable reflecting our knowledge:In this context, the mean will represent the real temperature (even if unknown), and the variance represents the sensor's inaccuracy.Because carries sensor noise that does not exist in the physical model, the predicted state also becomes fully epistemic. Even if the state's true physical variation across experiments is only driven by , our best possible inference of the future state must now expand to include our epistemic uncertainty regarding the sensor:4. Conclusion: Reconciling the ViewsThis reveals the ultimate power of the epistemic formulation: , , and are always treated as random variables in general, regardless of the origin of their randomness. The randomness captured by a variance matrix can be "real" (e.g., physical wind gusts driving ) or "perceived" (e.g., a deterministic temperature measured imperfectly by ). We use the exact same mathematical notation for both. The equations abstract away the origin of the uncertainty, leaving it entirely up to the user to interpret whether the variance represents physical reality or purely a lack of knowledge.Because we only ever observe one reality, and we observe it through noisy sensors, the ensemble statistics naturally become the exact measure of our epistemic uncertainty. The epistemic view serves as the most general framework: it allows us to interpret our predictions as the absolute best estimates available, whether based on precise physical characterizations or the limits of our current knowledge.5. The Epistemic View of the Sensor EquationTo complete this framework, we apply the exact same epistemic lens to the sensor equation:Here, , , and are epistemic random variables. Under this interpretation, they take on a very specific meaning: is a random variable representing our knowledge of the sensor measurement. Because it represents the sensor reading, its statistical variance explicitly captures the physical hardware noise of the sensor. , therefore, is not the raw sensor noise. Instead, it represents the sensor equation noise. It encapsulates our epistemic uncertainty regarding the measurement model itself—such as an imperfect mathematical representation of the sensor's physical mounting, unmodeled environmental perturbations, or geometric simplifications in . By isolating the hardware noise within the measurement variable () and the model uncertainty within the equation noise (), we establish a natural bridge to the Information Filter perspective. The sensor equation is not viewed as a forward prediction of a reading, but as an explicit source of inference for the state. Something that becomes clear by rearranging the equation. In this way, we isolate the informational contribution provided by the sensor:This formulation explicitly demonstrates that our updated knowledge of the observed state components () is epistemically derived: we take our noisy measurement knowledge () and subtract our uncertain knowledge of both the deterministic inputs () and the flaws in our own modeling framework ().6. The Epistemic Flow of State KnowledgeFinally, recognizing the epistemic nature of these equations requires us to explicitly trace the sequential source of our knowledge at each step of the filter.Because the equations track our evolving belief rather than just physical mechanics, the "state" variable represents different stages of inference depending on the equation:
In the process/prediction equation, the source of information for the state () is our posterior inference—the updated estimate derived in the previous step (). We project this past knowledge forward. In the sensor/observation equation, the source of information for the state () is our prior inference—the prediction just generated by the process equation ().

observability.html.title: Observability
observability.html.description: Observability is a fundamental concept in control theory and state estimation. It is defined as the ability to determine the state of a system on a given step, given measurements in that and following steps. If a system is observable, it means that by watching its inputs and outputs over a period of time, we can mathematically reconstruct its internal state.For an LTI system, the state and measurement equations are governed by constant matrices (, , , ). The system propagates as follows:State Equation:Measurement Equation:To understand how observability is determined, we can project the measurements forward in time and express them in terms of the initial state : Step : Step : Step : By gathering these sequential measurements into a single column vector, we can separate the terms dependent on the state from the terms dependent on the control inputs :Because the control inputs () are known, we can subtract them from the measurements. This reveals that we can only obtain the part of that projects onto the rows of the observability matrix.For an LTI system of order , the observability matrix is constructed by stacking the products of the measurement matrix and state transition matrix:The Observability Condition: If the rank of the observability matrix is equal to the number of states (), then the system is fully observable at step .In systems where the dynamics change over time (LTV) or are nonlinear, the constant matrices are replaced by time-dependent matrices or Jacobians evaluated at specific time steps (, ).For time-varying systems, the state transition matrices must be cascaded sequentially rather than raised to a power:Important Caveat for Nonlinear Systems:For a system that is not strongly nonlinear, this LTV formulation using linearized matrices (, ) can give a good idea of the observability. However, strictly speaking, it is only a measure of the local observability (observability in the immediate neighborhood of step ).The classical observability matrix provides a fundamental geometric baseline. It dictates whether the measurement axes, propagated through the system dynamics, eventually span the entire state space. This algebraic rank condition is an absolute, non-negotiable barrier: if , the system contains an unobservable subspace. In such cases, no amount of filtering, smoothing, or sensor fusion can recover the states that remain structurally decoupled from the observations.However, while full rank () is a strict mathematical prerequisite, it is frequently insufficient for practical implementation. The classical LTI and LTV formulations implicitly assume perfect state transitions and exact sensor mappings. In complex mechanical systems—such as multibody dynamics subject to unmodeled joint compliances, friction, or rigid-body approximations—this binary view fails to capture the physical reality of the estimation problem.To transition from the ontological question of "Is it observable?" to the epistemic question of "To what degree is it observable?", we must fully reintroduce the stochastic nature of our models.In the presence of equation modeling noise (), sensor uncertainty (, ), and noisy control inputs (), binary observability is replaced by the concept of the Stochastic Observability Gramian. Rather than a simple true/false rank condition, we evaluate the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) associated with the state given a sequence of future observations.As established in the Two Filter Information Smoother framework, the precision of our state estimate derived from future data is equivalent to the recursive backward propagation of information. The information pulled back from a future step is heavily modulated by the intervening dynamic uncertainty:This epistemic formulation bridges the classical and practical views by strictly matching the algebraic rank, while exposing the functional limitations caused by noise.The aggregated backward Information Matrix, , serves as the exact stochastic counterpart to . Because observations provide exactly zero information about structurally hidden subspaces, the mathematical ranks are strictly equivalent:If , then exactly eigenvalues of will be exactly zero. Consequently, the covariance matrix becomes mathematically undefined (infinite) along those unobservable directions, correctly representing unbounded epistemic ignorance.Why the Eigenspectrum is the Superior Metric:Practical observability is dictated not by the rank, but by the eigenspectrum of the Stochastic Gramian. The process noise acts as a lossy channel for information; the further into the future a measurement occurs, the more its informational value degrades before reaching . A system may be algebraically observable (full rank), but if the eigenvalues of its FIM are infinitesimally small, the corresponding state covariance expands massively. In practice, this renders the state functionally unobservable, buried beneath the noise floor.For strictly nonlinear systems, evaluating the local Jacobians (, ) requires a nominal state trajectory. Because the true state is unknown, we must linearize around our estimated states. However, computing the Stochastic Gramian backwards requires estimates of the state that depend on the Gramian itself, necessitating an iterative approach (an Iterated Extended Information Smoother).1. Initial Forward Pass:We first run a standard forward Extended Information Filter to obtain an initial nominal trajectory of state estimates and their forward information matrices .2. The Backward Pass (Information Accumulation):Using the forward estimates to linearize the Jacobians, we compute the backward variables recursively from down to :3. State Estimation (Smoothing Fusion):We cannot compute the backward state estimate directly as because if the system is unobservable, is singular. Instead, we compute the fully smoothed state by fusing it with the forward pass (which acts as a regularizing prior):4. Iteration and Convergence:The new smoothed trajectory represents our best epistemic belief of the physical states. We now use these improved states as the new linearization points to re-evaluate the Jacobians (, ) and re-run the backward pass. This process iterates until the change in the Stochastic Gramian () or the smoothed states falls below a convergence threshold, yielding the true practical observability of the nonlinear system.A critical limitation of classical linear theory arises when a nonlinear system is evaluated strictly by linearizing it around a single, stable equilibrium point. At this fixed state, the Jacobians (, ) remain constant. If the resulting classical observability matrix is rank-deficient at this point, linear theory strictly declares the system unobservable. However, this conclusion represents a "linearization trap"—it is only true if the system never actually leaves that exact equilibrium state.In the physical reality of a nonlinear system, as the state moves along a dynamic trajectory away from equilibrium, the Jacobians change continuously. This continuous evolution gives the system "richness," effectively rotating the measurement axes within the state space. By scanning the state space from these changing geometric perspectives, the varying Jacobians often couple previously hidden dimensions into the sensor outputs, rendering the system observable in motion even if it was unobservable at rest.The Stochastic Information Gramian naturally captures and quantifies this phenomenon because it evaluates observability over a dynamic trajectory rather than at a static tangency. If we examine the deterministic core of the aggregated backward Information Matrix over steps, it takes the approximate form of a sum of Fisher Information Matrices projected back to the initial time:Because the matrices inside this summation are evaluated at varying states along the trajectory, each term in the sum represents a different geometric projection. Even if an individual term at a specific step is algebraically rank-deficient, a subsequent term evaluated at a different state may possess a row space that covers the previously missing dimensions. Consequently, the aggregated sum can reliably build up to full rank (), mathematically demonstrating how the rich dynamics of the trajectory render the complete state space practically observable.

info_allowCollapsing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be collapsed

info_rightDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the right sidebar

info_leftDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the left sidebar

info_selector.description: CSS selector for an element. The feature will be placed relative to this element.

info_type.description: Will this feature be placed before, after, or inside (at the beggining or end).

info_featurePlacement.description: Where to place this feature on the page. (Relative to the selector)

info_sourcePath.description: The local path to the source .html file which will be included.

info_allowFoldingLists.description: Whether or not to allow lists to be folded

info_allowFoldingHeadings.description: Whether or not to allow headings to be folded

info_siteUrl.description: The url that this site will be hosted at

info_authorName.description: The name of the author of the site
